newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity ends mixed, backs off highs.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity ends mixed, backs off highs.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures ended mixed Tuesday, backing off morning highs that came with strong physical power prices and hot weather, industry sources said.

"We had a couple of late-day (downward) indicators -- Colstrip (generation unit) is coming back, capacity on the (Pacific) Intertie is being raised, and natural gas backed off," said on Western futures trader.
One of the two 700 megawatt (MW) coal-fired power generators that tripped off line Tuesday at the Colstrip power complex in Montana was seen back in service later today.

Colstrip unit 3 was in the process of resuming operations, while unit 4 may return to service Wednesday, sources said. The adjoining Colstrip units 1 and 2, rated at 330 MW each, were said to be operating normally.

Prices for peak power for the balance of August at the Palo Verde switchyard were said to be talked at $44.00-46.00 late Tuesday following trade as high as $47.00 per megawatt hour (MWh), the sources said.

In NYMEX futures, September Palo Verde (PV) finished up 12 cents at $31.16 after hitting a new contract high of $33.25 and trading as low as $31.05, while October ended down 20 cents at $22.97 following exchanges in a range of $22.90-23.85 per MWh.
Remaining PV deferreds finished down five to 12 cents.

September California Oregon Border (COB) futures settled down 10 cents at $24.25 following exchanges in a range of $24.15-25.05, while October ended up six cents at $22.20 after reaching a new contract high of $23.35 and a low of $22.15 per MWh.
NYMEX said an estimated total of 984 PV and 622 COB contracts traded Tuesday.

Western physical power prices soared Tuesday on hot, humid weather in parts of the West, with next-day firm, peak power at PV said to have traded as high as $95.00 per MWh from early Tuesday talk at $55.00-65.00 per MWh.

Separately, the operating limit on the Pacific Intertie transmission system will be increased to 6,900 MW from the current interim rating of 6,300 MW from 2400 PDT Tuesday, Bonneville Power Administration (BPA) said.

The spokeswoman for the federal agency which operates the intertie said only 6,650 MW of energy could be scheduled on the system after the capacity increase. The difference between the operating and scheduling limits was said to be a step to help manage curtailments due to loop flow problems.
The 6,900 MW limit will continue until the next seasonal operating plan is put together and reviewed by the Western System Coordinating Council.

Much of the western U.S. was predicted to feel sweltering heat through Thursday with the exception of Wyoming, Colorado and New Mexico, which were expected to experience much cooler than normal conditions.
In the six to 10 day forecasts, temperatures in the Southwest would cool toward more seasonal levels, while those in the Northwest would stay near to slightly above normal.
Also, electricity output from the 1,221 MW Palo Verde nuclear power unit 3 in Wintersburg, Ariz., held at 90 percent power early Tuesday for repairs to a condensate pump.
The unit was expected to return to full power within the next 48 hours, a spokesman for the plant said.
The adjacent 1,221 MW Palo Verde nuclear power unit 2 was operating at 91 percent of capacity as of early Tuesday as the unit coasts down to a scheduled refueling outage September 6.
Water flow into regional hydroelectric systems in the Northwest and Canada has been slowed in recent days to refill reservoirs for fish migration requirements.
((--Chris Reese, New York Power Desk +1 212 859 1627))
